section_summary: This section examines factional strains in Yoshida Shigeru’s Democratic Liberal Party and competing explanations for the January 1949 election results. It includes Kato Shizue’s account of the Social Democratic defeat and Richard L-G. Deverall’s criticism of occupation labor and information policies. A congressional inquiry asks about the safety of American sisters in Japan; the section ends with the opening of a despatch on the Democratic Party’s coalition dispute.

subfiles.title: Factions Within Democratic Liberal Party
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports factional strains within the Democratic Liberal Party following Yoshida’s third cabinet.
subfiles.summary: The despatch describes Old Guard, postwar leader, bureaucrat, and Shidehara factions, plus the likely entry of Inukai’s group. Sebald warns that cabinet appointments and the party’s enlarged membership complicate Yoshida’s leadership.

subfiles.title: The Yoshida Cabinet
subfiles.about: Describes factional dissatisfaction and cabinet appointments that could weaken Yoshida’s government.
subfiles.summary: Kuroki identifies competing party factions and disputes over the House speakership, cabinet posts, and coalition with Inukai’s Democrats. Pages 146 and 147 reproduce the same article.

subfiles.title: Cleavages Among the Democratic-Liberals
subfiles.about: Warns that coalition plans and internal party disputes may threaten government stability.
subfiles.summary: The editorial discusses resentment over Inukai’s prospective entry, excluded veteran leaders, and the difficulty of managing a greatly expanded party. Pages 148 and 149 reproduce the same clipping.

subfiles.title: Comments on Tokyo’s Despatch No. 94
subfiles.about: Summarizes and assesses a despatch on Japan’s January election.
subfiles.summary: Green reviews party realignment, Yoshida’s victory, Communist gains, election administration, and the Democratic Liberals’ governing difficulties. He generally accepts Spinks’s conclusions but doubts the prediction of a developing two-party system.

subfiles.title: Congressional inquiry concerning Notre Dame sisters in Japan
subfiles.from: Thomas J. Lane, House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Forwards Lena Carr’s request for an official assessment of conditions affecting sisters in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Requests an official reply about the sisters’ safety.

subfiles.title: Lena Carr’s inquiry about the sisters in Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether Communist activity might endanger American sisters working in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Carr asks about civil war, regime change, and the safety of sisters at Okayama and Hiroshima.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning conditions in Japan
subfiles.about: Responds to concerns that American sisters in Japan might face violence or internment.
subfiles.summary: Gross sees no present need for withdrawal and expects warning if conditions seriously deteriorate.

subfiles.title: Reasons for Social Democratic Party’s Defeat in January Election
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits and evaluates Kato Shizue’s explanation of her party’s election defeat.
subfiles.summary: Sebald summarizes Kato’s arguments about weak organization, unmet promises, occupation policy, Yoshida’s popularity, and Communist campaigning. He considers her account useful but biased by defeat, and argues that Communist gains also reflected voters’ response to a clear program.

subfiles.title: The Defeat of the Social Democratic Party and Its Reestablishment
subfiles.about: Explains the Socialist election defeat and proposes ways to rebuild the party.
subfiles.summary: Kato attributes defeat to unclear principles, factionalism, poor publicity, coalition compromises, and the burden of implementing occupation policies. She credits Yoshida’s appeal partly to resistance to the occupation and describes the Communists’ extensive publications, local services, organizing, and union influence. She urges Socialist reconstruction as a middle course against political extremes.

subfiles.title: Conversation with General Barr
subfiles.about: Recommends that Acheson speak with General Barr before Barr returns to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Butterworth also seeks Barr’s appearance before congressional foreign affairs committees.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting report on the occupation of Japan
subfiles.about: Sends a report urging changes to U.S. occupation policy and anti-Communist information work.
subfiles.summary: Deverall says occupation authorities have failed to counter Communist ideology effectively.

subfiles.title: Occupation of Japan
subfiles.to: War Department; State Department; Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Criticizes occupation economic, labor, and information policies as enabling Communist growth.
subfiles.summary: Drawing on his occupation labor posts, Deverall argues that inflation, weak price controls, employer financing of unions, and Soviet and Communist propaganda increased Communist influence. He alleges failures within occupation headquarters and calls for enforcement of trade union principles, review of economic policy, and a stronger Japanese-language information campaign.

subfiles.title: Buddies Incorporated
subfiles.about: Shows blind children with companion dogs.
subfiles.summary: Photographs depict children bonding with and caring for dogs.

subfiles.title: Japan on the Red Timetable
subfiles.about: Argues that Communist influence in Japanese unions and media requires a stronger democratic response.
subfiles.summary: Deverall recounts Communist labor organizing, demonstrations, publications, and alleged influence over Japanese media and unions. He credits MacArthur with stopping strike threats but faults occupation economic and information policy. He urges stricter labor and economic measures and wider public education. The magazine pages also contain unrelated verse and an anecdote.

subfiles.title: Look at Me!
subfiles.about: A fictional character waits in a diner while planning to rob a payroll messenger.
subfiles.summary: Ed Lacey nervously waits for Mark Suddard’s payroll trip.

subfiles.title: Democratic Party Attitude Toward the Coalition Cabinet
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Introduces Kojima Tetsuzo’s views on the Democratic Party split over coalition with Yoshida.
subfiles.summary: Kojima expects a lasting split and attributes Inukai’s coalition move to funding and leadership ambitions.
